title: Devlens Research Summary: Why mothers and newborns are still dying in Bangladesh
excerpt: A DGHS review of 2025 deaths finds bleeding after birth and birth asphyxia rising as causes, with many deaths at home or on the way to care. What it means for NGOs and donors.

image.alt: Pregnant women at a workshop in a BRAC birthing centre in Korail slum, Dhaka
image.credit: Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0

content:
Bangladesh cut maternal and newborn deaths sharply over two decades, and the gains have stalled. A government review of deaths recorded in 2025 shows the same few causes doing most of the damage, and shows where families and the health system are losing women and babies. This summary sets out what the review found and what it means for NGOs, donors and health programmes.

The source

The review is the National Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response (MPDSR) Progress and Highlights 2025, published by the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) in June. It was compiled by the Centre for Injury Prevention and Research, Bangladesh (CIPRB), with support from UNFPA, UNICEF and WHO, using DHIS-2 data from all 64 districts. Its findings were reported by The Daily Star on 22 November.

In 2025 the system recorded 1,252 maternal deaths and 5,403 newborn deaths. The review notes the real numbers are likely higher because many deaths go unreported. It analysed 315 maternal deaths and 547 newborn deaths from 11 districts in detail, and those cases are the basis for the cause and timing figures below.

Where the country stands

According to the Bangladesh Sample Vital Statistics 2023, the maternal mortality ratio is 136 deaths per 100,000 live births and the neonatal mortality rate is 20 per 1,000 live births. The 2030 Sustainable Development Goal targets are below 70 and 12. Bangladesh would need to roughly halve maternal deaths and cut newborn deaths by about 40% in the next five years to meet them.

Finding 1: bleeding after birth is getting worse as a share of deaths

Postpartum haemorrhage caused about 44% of the 315 maternal deaths analysed, up from 34% of 265 analysed in 2020. Eclampsia and pre-eclampsia together caused about 20%. Both are largely preventable. Bleeding can be managed with drugs, trained staff and blood. Pre-eclampsia can be caught with regular blood pressure checks during pregnancy.

Prof Ferdousi Begum, former president of the Obstetrical and Gynaecological Society of Bangladesh, told the paper the situation had not improved "because of persistent shortages of trained manpower." She linked eclampsia deaths mainly to late diagnosis and poor treatment.

Finding 2: birth asphyxia is the biggest killer of newborns

Birth asphyxia, when a baby does not get enough oxygen around birth, caused 43% of the 547 newborn deaths analysed, up from 36% in 2020. Prematurity caused 28%. Prof Mohammad Abdul Mannan, chairman of neonatology at Bangladesh Medical University, pointed to prolonged or obstructed labour, home births or births with untrained attendants, weak antenatal care and teenage pregnancy as the main risks.

Before death, 39% of babies had feeding problems, 34% had fast breathing and 17% moved little or not at all. These are danger signs that families and community health workers can be trained to spot.

Finding 3: most deaths happen after the birth, and many at home

  • About 66% of maternal deaths happened within six weeks after delivery, and 19% during childbirth.
  • About 42% of the women who died had given birth at home.
  • About 22% died at home and at least 18% died on the way to a facility.
  • About 45% of deliveries were attended by traditional birth attendants, many without formal training.
  • About 35% of the women received no postnatal care.
  • About 29% of newborn deaths happened at home.

Put together, these figures describe a gap in the hours and days after birth. A woman who delivers at home, starts to bleed and lives far from a facility that can transfuse blood has little margin. A newborn who struggles to breathe at home may never reach care at all.

What the government says it will do

DGHS Director General Prof Prabath Chandra Biswas said strengthening antenatal and postnatal care is central to the government's plan. He said the plan includes filling vacant posts and recruiting about 100,000 health workers, 80% of them women, who would visit households every two months. It also aims to place specialist doctors, technical staff and ultrasonography at upazila level.

This is a large commitment. It sits alongside other evidence of strain: on 24 November Prothom Alo reported that Faridpur Medical College Hospital holds about 1,425 patients a day in 500 beds, with most support posts unfilled. Recruitment on the scale promised would need money in the budget and a plan to keep women health workers in remote posts.

What the experts recommend

  • Measure blood loss at every delivery, keep essential medicines in stock and use the WHO E-MOTIVE rapid-response package for haemorrhage.
  • Keep blood banks, emergency surgery and referral systems working, with trained staff.
  • Hold regular antenatal check-ups with blood pressure monitoring to catch pre-eclampsia.
  • Increase antenatal visits and make sure trained professionals attend births.

What it means for NGOs and donors

Many of the gaps in the review are in places where NGOs already work: home births, community referral, and care after the mother and baby go home.

  • Postnatal visits. One in three women who died got no postnatal care. Community health worker and midwife programmes can target the first 48 hours and first week after birth, when most deaths occur.
  • Referral and transport. At least 18% of women died on the way to care. Emergency transport schemes, union-level referral links and pre-agreed blood donors can shorten that journey.
  • Birth attendants. With 45% of deliveries handled by traditional attendants, training them to recognise bleeding and newborn danger signs, and to refer early, remains useful while facility births grow.
  • Midwives. Donor-funded midwifery programmes are one of the most direct answers to the shortage of trained staff the experts describe.
  • Teenage pregnancy and family planning. Experts list teenage pregnancy and unplanned pregnancy as risk factors. Adolescent health and family planning work is part of the same problem.
  • Data. The review analysed deaths from only 11 districts, and reporting is incomplete. Support for death reviews in more districts would show where the gaps are worst.

Limits of the evidence

The cause and timing figures come from 315 maternal and 547 newborn deaths in 11 districts, not a national sample, so they may not reflect every region. Reported totals undercount deaths. The comparison with 2020 is based on smaller samples. The national ratios come from a separate source, the 2023 Sample Vital Statistics. Devlens has relied on The Daily Star's reporting of the review and has not seen the full document.

The bottom line

Women in Bangladesh are dying mostly of bleeding after birth, and newborns mostly of breathing failure at birth. Most of these deaths happen in the days after delivery, often at home or on the road. The causes are known and the fixes are well tested. The question is whether staff, blood and transport reach the places where births still happen at home.
